cards.source_title: Pydantic AI docs: Output (Tool Output, Native Output, Prompted Output, output validators)
cards.claim: Pydantic AI's default way to force structure is a special output tool whose parameters are the output JSON schema. Native structured output and prompt-only parsing are opt-in alternatives. This is the same mechanism as the Workflow StructuredOutput tool. BAML deliberately takes the third route (prompt plus parse; per its function-calling post, no JSON mode or constrained generation), so forced tool output is shared mainstream, not BAML-distinctive, and BAML's route is the minority one.
cards.evidence: Docs text only: tool output is the default; native output has the strongest enforcement but only on supporting models and with schema limits; prompted output is often the least reliable. Output retry budget defaults to 1, counted per output tool. No measurements.
cards.first_guess: No change. It confirms the harness already uses the mainstream forcing mode. If the design doc ever needs to justify relying on the forced tool call, the tool/native/prompted vocabulary is a ready frame, and SAP can be read as an answer to a problem (no tool-call validation layer) that Workflow already solves.

cards.claim: Tolerating malformed output is not unique to BAML. DSPy's JSONAdapter asks for structured outputs or JSON mode when the model supports it, then parses leniently (json_repair, then a regex for the first {...} block), casts each value to its annotated type, and raises AdapterParseError on a key mismatch. BAML's distinctive claim is narrower: schema-guided least-edit repair ('custom edit distance') rather than generic JSON repair. I did not read BAML's parser, so that difference is unverified.
cards.evidence: Code read in json_adapter.py: json_repair.loads, regex fallback, parse_value per annotated type, AdapterParseError, and a fall back to json_object mode if schema building fails. BAML side: its SAP post lists repairs for unquoted strings, trailing commas, misnamed keys and surrounding chatter. No head-to-head measurement of the two parsers exists in what I found.
cards.first_guess: Not relevant to Workflow scripts, since validation sits in the tool-call layer and scripts never parse model text. If the knowledge-store CLI ever ingests agent-authored JSON, a deterministic tolerant coercer needs no LLM and would not break the no-LLM-in-store rule. Strict rejection with a specific error is the honest default because it keeps agent mistakes visible.

cards.source_title: Boundary blog: Schema-Aligned Parsing (SAP) and its BFCL table
cards.quote: assume that the model will make mistakes
cards.claim: BAML's central claim is that repairing output locally with SAP beats both native function calling and a Python AST parser, so a parse-failure retry loop is not needed. Packaged as a technique it is distinctive; its relatives (DSPy json_repair, TypeChat's single repair) are looser. The post also rates constrained generation 2/5 (open-source only, grammars hard to maintain), says JSON mode is rigid with error rates often 10%+, and says retries add unbounded latency and cost.
cards.evidence: Vendor-run on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard dataset, n=1000 per model. Accuracy as function calling / Python AST / SAP: gpt-3.5-turbo 87.5/75.8/92; gpt-4o 87.4/82.1/93; claude-3-haiku 57.3/82.6/91.7; gpt-4o-mini 19.8/51.8/92.4; claude-3-5-sonnet 78.1/93.8/94.4; llama-3.1 7B (as written) n/a/60.9/76.8. Single benchmark, 2024-era models, no replication found. A companion Boundary post admits some BFCL assertions are ambiguous and were left unfixed. Constrained decoding and retries are not in the benchmark, so no number compares SAP against them.
cards.first_guess: Idea source only. The numbers use obsolete models and a vendor-run benchmark. The transferable principle (absorb output mistakes next to the parser instead of looping on retries) is already provided upstream of the script by forced tool-call validation. No action.

cards.source_title: BoundaryML/baml README, boundaryml.com homepage, docs v0 notice
cards.source_date: 2026-11-04 (repo last pushed 06:43 UTC per GitHub API)
cards.quote: BAML is the programming language for agents.
cards.claim: Correction to the prior assessment. 'Prompts as typed functions for app code' describes BAML v0. The current README and homepage pitch BAML v1 as a general programming language for agents (green threads, own stdlib, 'built-in tests / eval framework'). Neither page mentions schema-aligned parsing, retries, fallbacks, or any comparison with Pydantic or Instructor. Every BAML docs page I could reach (comparisons, testing, retry, fallback, optimisation, SAP) is stamped v0/legacy and I could not reach v1 docs, so BAML's comparative claims are legacy-version claims and may not describe the product as it is now.
cards.evidence: README and homepage: positioning text, no benchmarks; homepage says open source and pre-1.0. docs.boundaryml.com notice: the site documents v0, and v1 is a separate language in public beta. GitHub API: 9,475 stars, Apache-2.0, Rust, 372 open issues, pushed 2026-11-04 (active). Candidate v1 docs URLs returned 404.
cards.first_guess: Carry into the ideas document: do not cite BAML's v0 comparison pages as a description of the current product. FixFlow has no LLM application code, so v1's agent-language ambition has no landing here. An evaluation of BAML as an agent language would be a separate sweep.

cards.source_title: baml-diligence-eval: controlled benchmark of BAML versus raw Pydantic (third party)
cards.quote: All 116 Pydantic failures were the same failure mode
cards.claim: The only third-party measurement of BAML against a plain schema-in-prompt approach that I found. With retries off, BAML parsed 900/900 and OpenAI plus Pydantic parsed 784/900 (87.1%). All 116 failures were labelled 'schema-echo' by the author (as I read the label, the reply reproduced the schema block instead of data). So the measured gap tracks how the schema was rendered into the prompt, not parsing power. The comparison was against raw Pydantic, not Instructor (which reasks) or Pydantic AI.
cards.evidence: README: 1,800 calls, temperature 0.2, no retries, claude-3-haiku and gpt-4o-mini via OpenRouter, one task (job description to resume bullets), 95% Wilson intervals (bounds not printed). Adversarial 18/18 vs 17/18; multi-stage 50/50 vs 47/50. Stated limits: one domain, two models, n=100 per cell, latency confounded by prompt size (62-line JSON Schema vs 13-line BAML format). Author and affiliation unknown.
cards.first_guess: A prompt-hygiene item rather than an adoption case: do not paste a raw JSON Schema into brief prose when the forced tool already carries the schema. In any future brief test, include a schema-echo check (output equals the schema or a placeholder). Small, single-author evidence.

cards.source_title: LMQL docs: OpenAI models (limits); with Outlines and guidance READMEs
cards.quote: does not provide a way to obtain token distributions
cards.claim: Decoding-level enforcement (Outlines, guidance/llguidance, LMQL) works by masking tokens, which needs logit access that hosted chat APIs do not expose. LMQL's OpenAI doc says complex constraints 'may not be enforceable' on the Chat API. The guidance README says its guarantee holds 'so long as the backend LLM has full support'. Outlines' page claims 'Same code runs across OpenAI, Ollama, vLLM' and 'No parsing, no errors, no retries' but does not say how the guarantee is delivered on hosted backends. BAML's rejection of constrained generation for hosted models is therefore shared reality, not a distinctive insight, and this family does not apply to a Claude-driven harness.
cards.evidence: LMQL docs: Completions API logit_bias capped at 300 and top-5 logprobs; Chat API gives no token distributions. Guidance and Outlines READMEs/docs give no measured hosted-API results. LMQL repo shows 4.2k stars and the warning 'We do not continously test the main version'; I saw no last-commit date or release, so its maintenance status is unconfirmed.
cards.first_guess: No landing: the harness calls hosted Claude through Claude Code, where the forcing mechanism is the tool call, so token-level constraint libraries are out of scope. Value is as a correction: 'BAML does not use constrained decoding' describes the situation of every hosted-API user.

cards.source_title: JSONSchemaBench: evaluating constrained decoding with real-world JSON schemas (arXiv 2501.10868)
cards.quote: consistently improves the performance of downstream tasks up to 4%
cards.claim: Measured evidence on the constrained-decoding family that BAML rates 2/5. Across about 10K real schemas, Guidance, Outlines, llama.cpp, XGrammar, OpenAI and Gemini differ widely in schema coverage and compliance. Constrained decoding improved downstream accuracy by up to 4% over unconstrained on three reasoning tasks (open models). Hosted OpenAI and Gemini had near-perfect compliance but low coverage (OpenAI 0.29 on GitHub Easy), meaning they accept few real-world schemas. This cuts against a blanket claim that forcing structure hurts quality and supports keeping schemas simple.
cards.evidence: Guidance had the highest coverage on 6 of 8 sets and the lowest per-token time (about 6-9 ms vs 15-17 ms unconstrained). Outlines had the slowest grammar compilation (3.5 s and 8.1 s) and 0.06 compliance on GitHub Hard, mostly from timeouts, vs Guidance 0.69. GSM8K 83.8% vs 80.1% unconstrained. Authors caution OpenAI/Gemini numbers are not comparable with open-source engines (different models). I read the first 100,000 of 111,171 characters; the abstract does not name llguidance.
cards.first_guess: Supports keeping Workflow schemas inside the simple subset the contracts already use (object root, required within properties, small enums), because provider-side schema support is narrower than JSON Schema. No tool adoption.

cards.source_title: Let Me Speak Freely? Impact of format restrictions on LLM performance (arXiv 2408.02442), with dottxt rebuttal
cards.quote: Surprisingly, we observe a significant decline in LLMs reasoning abilities under format restrictions.
cards.claim: BAML's function-calling post cites this paper to argue schema constraints degrade quality. The abstract reports a decline in reasoning under stricter format restrictions. The effect is contested: dottxt re-ran three of its tasks on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and found structured generation equal or better, blaming unequal prompts between conditions, a JSON prompt that never mentioned JSON, and an LLM answer parser. The effect seems to depend on prompt parity and parser choice, so neither side is settled evidence for forced tool calls on Claude.
cards.evidence: Abstract only (read): stricter formats cause larger drops; it names no tasks or models. dottxt rebuttal (blog.dottxt.ai/say-what-you-mean.html, read), unstructured vs structured: GSM8K 0.77/0.78, Last Letter 0.73/0.77, Shuffle Objects 0.41/0.44. dottxt sells structured generation, so it has a stake. Neither side tested forced tool calls on Claude.
cards.first_guess: Two usable lessons, no adoption. (1) Where a brief needs reasoning plus a verdict, let the schema carry a free-text analysis field before the verdict enum rather than assuming the schema is free. (2) When brief tests exist, compare conditions with identical prompts and a deterministic checker, the thing the rebuttal says the paper lacked.

cards.source_title: Pydantic AI docs: models overview (FallbackModel), with DSPy ChatAdapter and BAML v0 retry/fallback pages
cards.quote: validation errors stem from the non-deterministic nature of LLMs
cards.claim: Pydantic AI separates two failure kinds. Provider failures (4xx/5xx, timeouts, rate limits, context overflow) fall back to the next model; structured-output validation errors do not and are retried on the same model. A custom fallback_on can also inspect the response (for example finish_reason). DSPy draws a similar line: ChatAdapter falls back to JSONAdapter only on AdapterParseError, while configuration errors and engine failures propagate. BAML v0: retry_policy retries network errors only, a fallback client is tried 'if it fails', and parse failures raise BamlValidationError carrying raw_output; whether a parse failure triggers retry or fallback is not stated. Built-in retries and fallbacks are thus shared with prior art; BAML adds declaring them in the language, and SAP in place of the parse-failure retry.
cards.evidence: Pydantic AI overview (read). DSPy chat_adapter.py (read): fallback skipped if output was already emitted, if already JSONAdapter, or if use_json_adapter_fallback is False (default True). BAML v0 retry-policy, fallback and error-handling pages (read, all stamped legacy). No measurements.
cards.first_guess: A design-doc rule to borrow, not code: a schema failure is retried at the same tier and never silently escalated to a stronger model; only infrastructure failures may change tier. That keeps tier assignment an orchestrator decision. Worth checking what agent() does when its internal validation retries are exhausted.

cards.source_title: Pydantic AI docs: overview, testing and evals pages (offline test models versus dataset evals)
cards.quote: runs entirely offline without calling an LLM
cards.claim: Prior art splits prompt-adjacent testing into two layers. Layer 1 tests the code around the model offline with a stand-in model: Pydantic AI TestModel and FunctionModel, Agent.override, capture_run_messages, and ALLOW_MODEL_REQUESTS=False so an accidental live call fails the test; guidance has a local Mock model. Layer 2 scores real model output against a dataset: Pydantic Evals (code-first Dataset, Case, Evaluators including LLM judges) and DSPy Evaluate with metrics. Pydantic AI says outright that layer 1 does not show whether answers are good; that is the job of evals.
cards.evidence: Pydantic AI overview, testing.md and evals.md (all read); guidance README (Mock model, grammar.match). Documentation only; no measurement, and no regression workflow is described by the evals page.
cards.first_guess: Gives the harness a vocabulary, since it has neither layer today. A layer-1 analog is a stub agent() returning canned objects so Workflow script control flow (gates, verdict routing, loops) can be tested without models. A layer-2 analog is a corpus of briefs with expected checks. Both need an owner decision on where such a runner lives, since scripts have no imports or filesystem.

cards.source_title: BAML docs (v0): BAML vs LangChain, vs Marvin, vs Pydantic, and Testing functions
cards.quote: Test your prompts instantly without API calls or mocking
cards.claim: BAML's testing pitch: test blocks live in .baml beside the function; assertions are Jinja expressions (@@assert halts at the first failure, @@check records a named result); they run from the VS Code playground or baml-cli test (filter, --parallel) and feed the prompt optimiser. Against prior art, in-language tests plus a playground are distinctive packaging; offline fake-model tests (Pydantic AI, guidance Mock) and dataset evals (Pydantic Evals, DSPy) are shared ideas. The BAML pages say Instructor has 'no included testing capabilities' (true of the Instructor docs I read, not of the field). I could not reconcile 'without API calls': the testing and test-reference pages show tests bound to real clients, never say whether a run consumes tokens, and mention no LLM judge.
cards.evidence: baml-vs-langchain, baml-vs-marvin, baml-vs-pydantic, testing-functions and ref/baml/test pages (all read, all v0-stamped). Instructor README and docs: testing not covered. Whether the claim means prompt preview rather than test execution is unresolved from docs alone.
cards.first_guess: Idea only: deterministic assertions over structured output (enum in an allowed set, evidence string matching 'path:line - quote', latency bound) are what the existing output contracts already allow, so brief regression could start as cases plus such checks with no framework. Resolve the 'without API calls' ambiguity before anyone relies on it.

cards.source_title: BAML docs: Prompt Optimization (Beta), GEPA over test blocks
cards.quote: lots of examples in the form of tests
cards.claim: Automatic prompt tuning is shared with DSPy, not BAML-distinctive. BAML's beta optimiser is GEPA, which the BAML page attributes to DSPy's creators, run over BAML test blocks scored by @@assert/@@check plus built-in accuracy, token and latency measures with adjustable weights. DSPy offers the same family (optimisers, Evaluate, GEPA); its landing page shows an F1 0.41 to 0.63 example with no stated dataset. BAML's page lists its own limits: single functions only, only prompt text and type descriptions editable, and all failures treated alike so a provider 500 can penalise a good prompt. It gives no result numbers.
cards.evidence: BAML prompt-optimization page (read): inputs, outputs, resumable .baml_optimize state, listed limitations, no measured improvement. DSPy home page (read): GEPA described as tuning prompts until quality converges, F1 example only.
cards.first_guess: No optimiser: it needs the test corpus first, which the harness lacks. The transferable requirement for any future brief-test runner is to classify infrastructure failures (provider errors, timeouts) apart from output failures, so a flaky provider is never scored as a bad brief.

cards.source_title: DSPy home page: saving optimised programs (and prompt versioning across the prior art)
cards.claim: Prompt versioning is not a differentiator anywhere in this prior art. DSPy saves an optimised program to a file (the 'v2' in the example filename is a naming convention, not a versioning feature). BAML prompts are source files in the repo, and its optimiser page tells users to version the prompt so they can revert. The Instructor, Pydantic AI, TypeChat, Outlines and LMQL pages I read say nothing about prompt versioning. BAML's claim reduces to 'prompts are code under version control', which any file-based brief already satisfies.
cards.evidence: Absence of content on each page read, which does not prove those projects have no versioning features. Pydantic's hosted Logfire offerings and Boundary's hosted tooling were not checked.
cards.first_guess: Nothing to adopt. Briefs already live in git; a run record can cite the brief's commit SHA, as the ship plan is already cited '@ 3415b5e'.

cards.quote: Based on the format used by BAML
cards.claim: The one BAML idea another major framework has copied is the compact, commented, type-style rendering of an output schema inside the prompt. DSPy's BAMLAdapter reuses only that rendering and inherits JSONAdapter's parsing; it imports nothing from BAML and has no SAP. BAML says its format cuts schema tokens by about 80%, from one example (roughly 180 vs 35 tokens). The third-party eval saw 62 lines of JSON Schema vs 13 lines.
cards.evidence: baml_adapter.py (read): docstring credits BAML's JSON formatter, helper functions render Pydantic models to compact layouts, parse is inherited. The 80% figure comes from BAML's why-baml page (single example, vendor). Line counts come from the baml-diligence-eval README. No token measurement across tasks.
cards.first_guess: Small and optional: if a brief restates its output contract in prose alongside the forced schema, a compact type-style listing is cheaper to read than JSON Schema. The forced tool's own schema is outside our control, so the saving applies only to prose restatements. Not worth a change on its own.

cards.source_title: TypeChat source: typescript/src/typechat.ts (repair loop), with Instructor retry docs
cards.quote: The JSON object is invalid for the following reason:
cards.claim: The reask family bounds and shapes its loop the same way. TypeChat validates against the schema, then appends the rejected reply plus the validator's message and asks for a revised object, at most once; a JSON parse error or a reply with no braces gets no repair. Instructor reasks on validation failure with the error text (max_retries is a count; README example uses 3), records failed_attempts, and its docs warn that the product of retry limits is only an upper bound on HTTP calls and that token_budget is 'a retry budget, not a hard per-request limit'. BAML's contrast is that retries add unbounded latency and cost. The shared idea is that the validator's specific error text is the repair signal.
cards.evidence: typechat.ts (read): attemptRepair defaults true, one repair, a validateInstance hook can add checks beyond the schema. Instructor retrying doc and README (read). Pydantic AI output retries default to 1 (see P-01). No measurement of how often reasks succeed.
cards.first_guess: Two cheap ideas. Put specific constraints in the schema (enums, patterns) so the validator's message names the fault. Ask whether Workflow exposes the count of StructuredOutput rejections per agent() call, since a brief that is rejected often is a defective brief and the count is the cheapest brief-quality signal. Per the orchestrator's context scripts see only the validated object, so this is likely unobservable today.

notes: The fetch tool returns model-extracted summaries, not raw pages; quotes are as presented and not checked against raw HTML. Every BAML docs page I could reach is stamped v0/legacy and I found no v1 docs, so BAML's retry, test and SAP claims are unverified for v1. No independent benchmark of SAP against Instructor or Pydantic AI turned up; the one third-party number (P-05) is one task, two small models. Nothing bears on (d). The prior assessment holds for (a) and (b): the yield is ideas, not the tool.
title: Prior art BAML cites or competes with
